paper_title: Search From the Start: Search-Native Pretraining for Language Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Modern language models (LMs) are increasingly deployed with access to search tools at inference. Yet pretraining remains predominantly focused on predicting static text, with search capabilities typically introduced during post-training. We propose Search-Native Pretraining as a practical route to teach search capability during pretraining from ordinary text corpora. Specifically, we augment pretraining corpus at scale with web-search queries and retrieve web response using a local index. Training on this augmented corpus teaches models to generate search calls and incorporate retrieved evidence during language modeling. Across Wikipedia and DCLM-Edu corpora and 360M to 3.3B parameter scales, search-pretrained models ("QueryLM") show improved performance on knowledge-intensive tasks and higher steerability toward the retrieved evidence. Crucially, their advantage persists after supervised fine-tuning of both search-pretrained and conventionally pretrained models, indicating that the tested post-training procedures do not fully recover the capabilities developed during pretraining. Throughout our experiments, we find that a 1.4B QueryLM consistently beats or matches the performance of a FLOP-matched 3.3B baseline model across all knowledge intensive tasks. These results establish search-pretraining as a practical way to develop foundational search capabilities during pretraining. We release the training artifacts, including model checkpoints and data.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Language models (LMs) have finite capacity to store factual knowledge in their parameters (Morris et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2026a), which can limit their performance on knowledge-intensive tasks. This poses particular challenge for smaller models, as facts that cannot be inferred from general patterns must be memorized during pretraining (Allen-Zhu & Li, 2024). Even when successfully encoded, knowledge in weights can become outdated as real-world facts change (Vu et al., 2023). Teaching an LM to search address these limitations by allowing factual knowledge to remain externally retrievable, with sources that can be updated without retraining the model. Prior work has explored several ways to incorporate retrieved knowledge at inference time (Lazaridou et al., 2022; Nakano et al., 2022; Parisi et al., 2022; Shuster et al., 2022; Asai et al., 2023; Schick et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2023; Jin et al., 2025). These capabilities are typically introduced during post-training (OpenAI et al., 2025; Dong et al., 2026; Kang et al., 2026), after the model has been pretrained to predict the next token without access to search. However, recent work demonstrates the benefits of early exposure to capability-relevant data during pretraining Zhang et al. (2025); Baek et al. (2026); Minder et al. (2026). Yet scaling such data to develop new capability during pretraining remains challenging, often requiring practitioners to rely on limited or synthetically generated data Gunasekar et al. (2023); Shao et al. (2024). We therefore ask: Can ordinary pretraining documents be augmented at scale to teach downstream capability such as search, while preserving the original next-token prediction objective? In particular, we want an LM to use search to access diverse and evolving knowledge sources, such as the internet. To teach the search ability during pretraining, we augment the training corpus with inline web-search tool calls and corresponding web-retrieved evidence that help predict the original document continuation. These augmentations demonstrate when to seek information beyond the available text, what to search for, and how to use the returned evidence to predict the continuation. Together, they form our Search-Native Pretraining approach. We construct search-augmented pretraining corpora from the knowledge-rich Wikipedia corpus and DCLM-Edu, which represents realistic pretraining setting. The augmented DCLM-Edu corpus contains over 100B tokens of document text, search queries, and retrieved responses. Using these corpora, we train QueryLM models from scratch at scales from 360M to 3.3B parameters. When search is available, QueryLM improves on knowledge-intensive tasks compared with FLOP-matched baselines (Section 5.1). Our 400M model with search also exceeds the average QA performance of SmolLM3-3B evaluated without search, despite using approximately 6,700 times less pretraining compute (Figure 1). The advantage over FLOP-matched baselines persists after both models undergo search-augmented finetuning, showing that the tested post-training recipe does not fully recover the benefit of learning search during pretraining (Section 5.1). Beyond answering more questions correctly, QueryLM more readily adjusts its predictions to supplied evidence, including evidence that contradicts facts seen during training (Section 5.2). General capabilities remain broadly comparable after search fine-tuning (Section 5.3), while our ablations examine how retrieval quality, response length, and insertion frequency affect performance and training cost (Section 6). These results support Search-Native Pretraining as scalable approach to teaching models to search for and use external information from the start of training.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: LM knowledge retention. Prior work has explored the limits of factual knowledge acquisition in language model parameters (Kandpal et al., 2023; Morris et al., 2025), highlighting challenges due to task feature interference (Huang et al., 2026a), reduced model plasticity (Kim et al., 2025; Springer et al., 2025), and forgetting (Liao et al., 2024; Luo et al., 2025). These challenges persists when the acquired knowledge becomes outdated and requires post-hoc editing (Lazaridou et al., 2021; Gu et al., 2024). Proposed mitigation includes data selection to prioritize learnable facts (Mindermann et al., 2022; Ye et al., 2026), modified parameter updates for reduced interference and easier editing (Wang et al., 2023; Ghosal et al., 2025), increasing model plasticity (Chen et al., 2024), and complementing parametric knowledge with externally retrieved information (discussed below). Building on these efforts, we address the limitation of parametric knowledge by pretraining an LM to fill in the knowledge gap through search and ground its generation on retrieved passages. External knowledge base. Prior work improves LMs on knowledge-intensive tasks by equipping them with external knowledge or tools. Inference-time or post-training approaches provide access to API-based tools or search engine during generation (Lazaridou et al., 2022; Nakano et al., 2022; Parisi et al., 2022; Shuster et al., 2022; Asai et al., 2023; Schick et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2023; Jin et al., 2025). Among these work, Toolformer (Schick et al., 2023) is particularly relevant to our approach, as it injects tool call demonstrations inline and fine-tunes an LM to issue relevant tool calls. Pretraining-focused efforts have explored jointly trained retrievers (Guu et al., 2020) or specialized layer to attend to retrieved information (Borgeaud et al., 2022). More recent approaches, such as LMLM (Zhao et al., 2025) and CoLMLM (Feldman et al., 2026), build an explicit entity-based key-value stores from training or downstream task data and trains an LM to query these stores. Unlike past methods, QueryLM learns to issue flexible search queries during pretraining from scratch, without architectural modification or an explicit entitybased key-value store. Pretraining data augmentation. Previous studies have shown the benefits of introducing downstream capability-relevant data earlier during pretraining (Akter et al., 2025b; Zhou et al., 2026), encoding desired behavior such as instruction-following ability (Cheng et al., 2024), reduced toxicity (Maini et al., 2025), higher steerability (Gao et al., 2025), improved reasoning (Akter et al., 2025a; Ruan et al., 2025), knowledge synthesis (Huang et al., 2026b). We similarly find that early exposure to search demonstrations in Search-Native Pretraining yields benefits that persist through post-training.

sections.title: 3 SEARCH-NATIVE PRETRAINING
sections.content: Search-Native Pretraining trains language model to issue search queries and incorporate retrieved evidence into subsequent generation. We construct demonstrations of these interactions by augmenting the training documents with search queries and externally retrieved evidence, while preserving the original document text. Figure 3: Document annotation example with inline search queries and retrieved documents.

sections.title: 3.1 WHEN AND WHAT TO SEARCH
sections.content: For each document, we identify set of search query insertion points = {a1, ..., ak}, each ai separating prefix pi, which sets the context motivating search, from suffix si, the original document continuation. good insertion point follows the prefix pi that naturally motivates search query qi, containing specific and relevant keywords from pi to retrieve useful context ri (Figure 3). We denote the collections of queries and retrieved responses as = {qi}k i=1 and = {ri}k i=1, respectively. Extending prior work (Zhao et al., 2025), which places insertion points before an entitys associated value (e.g., between Dante Alighieri was born in and May 1265), we consider more general insertion locations, such as immediately after specific term mention without linked value (e.g., placed after Dante Alighieri ) or positions where relevant information depends on distant context (e.g., between Dante Alighieri, [...], originally titled his masterwork and La Commedia). We use an LM to identify suitable insertion points and generate corresponding search queries. To efficiently annotate the pretraining corpus at scale, we first fine-tune small annotator model (Mϕ) and then use the trained annotator to augment the full corpus. Annotator model. We create small search-augmented dataset (Dseed) from an initial pool of 10,000 Wikipedia documents, annotated using GLM-5.2 (GLM-5-Team et al., 2026) as the teacher model. We prompt the teacher to identify insertion points before specific facts that could benefit from external retrieval, such as names, dates, and quantities. The teacher first identifies candidate insertion locations using the entire document but subsequently generates search query given only the corresponding left context. Query generation therefore uses the same available text as at inference. To remove insertions with failed or empty search result, we retrieve and clean search responses for each search query (process detailed in Section 3.2). Finally, we fine-tune Gemma 4 E4B (Gemma Team et al., 2026) on Dseed to produce the search query annotator, Mϕ. Further details on annotator training are given in Section A.1. Annotating pretraining corpus. For efficient search query insertion at pretraining scale, we process each sequence of length with Mϕ, the fine-tuned annotatir model, in single causal forward pass and compute query insertion scores following each i-th sequence token xi as πi(x) = Pr (<WEB-QUERY> x1:i) , = 1, . . . , T, where πi(x) is the probability of inserting search query immediately after token xi. Positions with πi(x) exceeding threshold τ [0, 1] form the final insertion set = {i {1, . . . , } πi(x) τ } = {a1, . . . , ak}. Candidate insertion positions can therefore be scored in parallel within each document. Our approach for sampling search insertion points refer to augmentation strategy in Schick et al. (2023). Finally, Mϕ generates query qi for each ai given corresponding prefix pi until the closing delimiter. These queries are then passed to the search response retrieval pipeline (Section 3.2). Insertion filtering. For pretraining corpus, we use τ = 0.05 as an initial filtering method to restrict the number of search queries inserted per document and drop low-quality search queries. We then do additional filtering using ROUGE-1 F1 overlap between the retrieved response ri and the original continuation si, using lexical overlap as proxy for relevance. The filtering threshold values and the filtering protocol are given in Section A.1.

sections.title: 3.2 SIMULATING WEB RESPONSE DURING PRETRAINING
sections.content: To simulate realistic and cost-efficient web-response, we use BM25 index over Sphere (Piktus et al., 2022), public dataset containing broad collection of 134M web documents. We consider candidate indexes over different corpus based on retrieval coverage and storage requirements, detailed in Section 6.2 and Section A.1. For each search query qi, we retrieve the top-10 scoring raw passages and select sentences with the most keyword stem overlap with the query, producing the web response ri used in training corpus annotation. The choice of how much retrieved information to retain introduces trade-off: shorter search response reduces training overhead but may remove relevant information, and cleaning the raw passage using an LLM may help select more query-relevant information but incurs higher data preparation cost. We evaluate the impact of training with web-response of different lengths and cleaning approach in Section 6.3 and Section 6.4.

sections.title: 3.3 PRETRAINING OBJECTIVE
sections.content: We train language models autoregressively on the annotated pretraining corpus. Given an annotated sequence of length (cid:101)T = and indices IR {1, . . . , (cid:101)T } for web-response tokens (i.e., ri and <WEB-RESPONSE> tokens), the training objective is L(θ) = (cid:101)T (cid:88) t=1 1[t / IR] log pθ(xt x<t). The model therefore is trained with next-token prediction objective on the original document text, search queries qi, and the special token <WEB-QUERY>, while masking the loss on web response tokens ri. This allows the model to condition the original document continuation on the web-response but avoids explicitly training it to reproduce the web response.

sections.title: 4.1 PRETRAINING SETUP
sections.content: Pretraining corpora. We pretrain models using Search-Native Pretraining on two corpora: Wikipedia and DCLM-Edu (Allal et al., 2025). Wikipedia provides compact, knowledge-rich setting for controlled experiments. DCLM-Edu extends the study to more diverse web text, testing whether the benefits persist beyond encyclopedic documents. Both corpora use the annotation pipeline described in Section 3, with the same annotation model. See Appendix Section A.2 for data preprocessing details. Baselines. For each of QueryLM across varying scales, we pretrain baseline model with the same architecture on original document text without search augmentation. We approximately match each baselines pretraining FLOPs to the corresponding QueryLM , including computation on retrieved response tokens despite their exclusion from the loss during Search-Native Pretraining (see Section A.2 for detail). We include LMLM (360M) and Co-LMLM (400M) models off-the-shelf as our baselines. Our 360MQueryLM trained on Wikipedia provides the closest comparison with LMLM, and our 400M-QueryLM (overtrained) on DCLM-Edu is compared with Co-LMLM trained on FineWeb. Model architectures and training budgets. For Wikipedia, we train decoder-only Transformers from scratch with 360M parameters using the SmolLM2 configuration (Allal et al., 2025), to have the closest match to LMLM baseline. Wikipedia QueryLM is trained on 33.4B tokens total over four epochs, with 4.01B tokens from original document tokens and 4.33B from search augmentation per epoch. For DCLM-Edu, we train nanochat configurations from scratch at 400M, 1.4B, and 3.3B parameters, excluding value embeddings. The 400M, 1.4B and 3.3B QueryLM are trained on 10.6B, 44.0B, and 99.8B tokens, 6.8B, 28.2B and 64.0B tokens from original document tokens (approx. 20 per parameter). We include deliberately over-trained 400M DCLM-Edu QueryLM (65.1B document tokens, 101.5B processed) to support comparison with Co-LMLM trained on FineWeb. Further architecture details, optimization settings, and training budgets are given in Section A.2.

sections.title: 4.2 SUPERVISED FINE-TUNING
sections.content: After pretraining, we fine-tune both QueryLM and the FLOP-matched baselines to develop user-assistant conversation behavior. We use two different supervised fine-tuning (SFT) mixtures to answer different questions. First, we perform standard SFT on subsample of the Dolci dataset, which includes search mixture, following the SFT setup of Olmo 3 (Olmo et al., 2026). Since many of the search traces in Dolci exceed our context length, we add our own search traces on SmolTalk conversations in an equal ratio. This setup tests whether QueryLM retains its advantage in the typical pipeline, where search is only introduced in post-training. Second, we introduce Search SFT, which uses much higher proportion of search-augmented data. The Search SFT mixture contains 52,806 conversations from SmolTalk (Allal et al., 2025) and SmolTalk2, covering general chat skills and tool calling. We additionally augment selected SmolTalk conversations with search interactions generated by our annotation model. The main goal is to evaluate whether the advantages Search-Native Pretraining can be fully recovered in posttraining with search-heavy data distribution. Further training details are provided in Section A.3.

sections.title: 4.3 EVALUATION
sections.content: Tasks. We consider TriviaQA (Joshi et al., 2017), NQ-Open (Kwiatkowski et al., 2019), PopQA (Mallen et al., 2023), and WebQuestions (Berant et al., 2013) as factual knowledge probing tasks (Factual QA), as well as HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018), 2WikiMultiHopQA (Ho et al., 2020), MuSiQue (Trivedi et al., 2022), and Bamboogle (Press et al., 2023) for multi-hop question answering (Multi-hop) using the Search-R1 evaluation suite (Jin et al., 2025). To assess factual grounding, we use on FreshQA (Vu et al., 2023) for time-sensitive factual question answering, and HaluEval (Li et al., 2023) and RAGTruth (Niu et al., 2024) for faithfulness to supplied evidence in hallucination-prone settings. Lastly, we evaluate QueryLM on general language understanding and commonsense reasoning benchmarks. Task details are included in Section A.4.1. Prompting. The base models are given four-shot search demonstration for all QA tasks. LMLM and Co-LMLM emit their own search queries to retrieve relevant values, and our FLOP-matched baseline uses its corresponding QueryLM search queries and retrieved results. After Search SFT, both QueryLM and FLOP-matched baselines are evaluated zero-shot and use their own search queries. Search is triggered for both base and SFT models with an injected <WEB-QUERY> in the beginning of model generation. Both base and SFT models are given budget of 1 look-up for factual QA and 2 look-ups for multi-hop QA. We report % correct answer is contained given the 24-token generation budget for base models, and LLM-judged accuracy with 64 token generation budget for SFT models. Prompt examples are included in Section A.4.3. For each metric, we report the 95% confidence intervals with bootstrap over questions. Retrieval source. For fair comparison with LMLM, which indexes its Wikipedia training corpus as the external knoweldge base, our Wikipedia-trained QueryLM (360M) uses BM25 index over Wikipedia. Similarly, our DCLM-Edu-trained QueryLM (400M) uses BM25 index over Fineweb-Edu and Wikipedia to match Co-LMLMs retrieval corpus. However, QueryLM can flexibly switch to weblike retrieval source, we report our main results including retrievals from Tavily, an API-based search engine. In Section 6.2, we demonstrate that switching to more realistic retrieval source like Tavily improves the model performance for both QueryLM and the FLOP-matched baselines.

With standard SFT, QueryLM retains much of its base performance (Figure 5, right). Even under the Search SFT recipe, with high proportion of search demonstrations, fine-tuned baselines do not fully recover the benefit of search pretraining, especially at smaller model scales (Figure 5, middle). sections.title: 5.2 QUERYLM USES RETRIEVED CONTEXT TO UPDATE ITS ANSWERS
sections.content: To investigate whether QueryLM grounds its predictions on retrieved evidence than on facts stored in its parameters, we measure its sensitivity to supplied evidence in controlled setting, then evaluate whether the increased sensitivity translates to improvement on downstream tasks. Updating knowledge based on counterfactual context. We first sample 1000 stated facts in DCLMEdu training documents and measure the model preference between ground-truth and plausible-butwrong (counterfactual) values, under retrievals supporting either options. For instance, we test if the counterfactual retrieval that falsely identifies Albert Einsteins birth-year as 1889 (correct: 1879) increases the models preference for 1889. We use GPT-oss-120B (OpenAI et al., 2025) to edit the original ground-truth relevant evidence to instead support the counterfactual values. Model preference is measured using the log-probability difference between the original and counterfactual values, log (original) log (counterfactual). We find that both supporting and counterfactual evidence increase QueryLM preference for the corresponding values more strongly than for the baseline models (Figure 6a). See Section A.5.2 for detailed setup and discussion. Generation grounded on relevant evidence. We further evaluate QueryLM context-following ability across the eight QA tasks using either the original ground-truth supporting and the edited counterfactual context (Figure 6b). To assess context following ability independently of query generation ability, we hold search queries fixed across QueryLM and FLOP-matched baselines. Retrieval uses BM25 over Sphere. Details of setting are discussed in Section A.5.2. QueryLM performs worse in closed-book setting, but is better at predicting the answer supported by supplied evidence, especially under counterfactual contexts. These results suggest that QueryLM relies more strongly on retrieved evidence. Additional evaluations on factual-groundedness benchmarks, including FreshQA, HaluEval, and RAGTruth, show similar trends (Appendix, Section A.5).

sections.title: 5.3 GENERAL CAPABILITIES
sections.content: For completeness, we evaluate QueryLM on general language understanding and commonsense reasoning in closed-book setting (Appendix Section A.5.3, Table 13). QueryLM base model slightly underperforms the FLOP-matched baselines, whereas the two are comparable after SFT, with mixed results across tasks. Search pretraining preserves general capabilities, but its advantage on search-based tasks does not translate into consistent improvements in closed-book reasoning.

sections.title: 6.1 HOW EFFECTIVE ARE QUERYLM ’S SEARCH QUERIES?
sections.content: We assess QueryLM and FLOP-matched baselines search query generation ability by comparing their downstream task performances using their own queries after Search SFT versus queries generated by stronger model, Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 (Team, 2025). This allows us to assess the effectiveness of self-generated queries, and whether stronger query generation can narrow the performance gap between QueryLM and baselines. Both settings use BM25 over Sphere for retrieval. Across model scales, replacing self-generated queries with Qwen-generated queries results in smaller performance gains for QueryLM than for the FLOP-matched baselines (Figure 7), suggesting that QueryLM generates more effective search queries. When the query source is fixed, QueryLM also outperforms the baselines at both 400M and 1.4B scales. However, this trend reverses at the 3.3B scale, potentially due to stronger parametric knowledge and in-context reasoning ability at larger scales.

sections.title: 6.3 HOW DOES TRAINING-TIME SEARCH CONTEXT AFFECT PERFORMANCE?
sections.content: We construct two search response variants for training data augmentation using an LM summarizer (Gemma 4 E4B): summaries of raw retrieved documents (LM-summarized) and summaries of the training documents themselves, which contain explicit ground-truth value asked for by the search query (oracle). The former tests the benefit of cleaner retrieval context, while the latter examines the effect of training on highly relevant evidence and models generalization beyond this controlled setting. We compare both against the original Wikipedia-trained 360M QueryLM and FLOP-matched baseline (Standard). Without search context (No context), Oracle exhibits the highest perplexity on 400 held-out documents original tokens, followed by QueryLM and LM-summarized  (Table 1)  . Perplexity drops slightly across all variants with the models inference-time queries and context (Live). With the original search annotations (Orig.), both Oracle and LM-summarized perplexity drops below QueryLM s, indicating greater reliance on the retrieved context. However, their stronger context reliance does not translate to improved performance on downstream QA (QA with search) and general benchmark (General), suggesting limited generalization to different retrieval setting (BM25 retrieval over Sphere).

sections.title: 6.4 CAN WE REDUCE TRAINING-TIME SEARCH RESPONSE LENGTH AND QUERY FREQUENCY?
sections.content: Longer responses and more frequent searches increase the amount of retrieved information available during pretraining, but also increase training cost. We examine two ways to reduce this overhead: shortening the retrieved context and limiting the number of query insertions. In the first variant, we limit the response length from 600 (our default) to 50 characters, which reduces the added sequence length and may also remove information useful for predicting the continuation. In the second variant, we retain only the two insertions per document with the highest response-continuation overlap. We find that both variants substantially reduce the amount of search augmentation while still retaining reasonable search capability useful for downstream performance  (Table 2)  . These results suggest that context length and insertion frequency offer ways to trade performance for lower training cost.

sections.title: 6.5 WHAT IS THE COST OF SEARCH-NATIVE PRETRAINING?
sections.content: The annotation phase scans the training corpus of size and adds A-many queries of length ℓq, adding Aℓ more tokens to training corpus, where ℓ is the size of query and response tokens. The data preparation is done once per corpus and can be reused across models. During inference, cost scales linearly with the number of search-calls, adding kℓ for rounds of search and retrievals. Number of search queries (A), tokens per query (ℓ), and the number of queries at inference (k) are hyperparameters that can be tweaked to reduce cost, whose impact is discussed in Section 6.3 and Section 6.4. See Table 14 in Appendix Section A.5.5 for summary table.

sections.title: 7 CONCLUSION
sections.content: Search-Native Pretraining aims to teach LMs two complementary skills during pretraining: what to search for and how to use retrieved evidence to continue generation, alongside the standard language modelling objective. Our results show that QueryLM acquires these capabilities, achieving higher performance on knowledge-intensive tasks with search and grounding its predictions more effectively in supplied evidence. The difference in the closed-book evaluations shows that the models are also successful in reframing much of the memorization in pretraining through the search objective. Together, these findings suggest that integrating search into pretraining can complement smaller models parametric memory by training them to access and use external knowledge effectively.

sections.title: A APPENDIX
sections.content: A.1 DATA ANNOTATION Creating the seed data. We construct Dseed from the first 10,000 English Wikipedia articles in the November 2023 snapshot that contain between 2,000 and 9,000 characters. GLM-5.2 annotates each document in two passes. It first reads the full document and marks where search could help predict an upcoming fact, such as name, date, or quantity. It then generates search query at each position using only the preceding 1,600 characters (referred to as pi in the main text). This separates the choice of where to search from query generation, reducing the risk of including the answer in the query. For each query, we retrieve passages with BM25 over FineWeb-Edu. We remove duplicate passages and passages for which at least 35% of word trigrams also occur in the source article. We keep the five highest-ranked remaining passages, truncated to approximately 900 characters each. Gemma-4-E4Bit compresses them into one to three sentences. This seed-data pipeline uses LLM compression over FineWeb-Edu; the later pretraining corpus annotation uses simple CPU-based cleaning over Sphere for scalability. We apply no additional relevance filter for queries: preliminary experiments showed that heavily filtering Dseed decreased the search query emission rate of the annotator. The final set contains approximately 20 search queries per document. We split train and validation data into 9:1 ratio for Mϕ fine-tuning. Annotator model training setup. We fine-tune Gemma 4 E4B-it (Gemma Team et al., 2026) on the training split of Dseed using LoRA with rank 16, α = 32, and dropout 0.05. Adapters are applied to the text decoders attention and feed-forward projections. We train for three epochs using AdamW, peak learning rate of 2 104, 3% warmup, cosine decay, and an effective batch size of 32 sequences. Each training sequence is one annotated document, preceded by an instruction describing when and how to search. Sequences are truncated on the right at 4,096 tokens. <tool_call> and <tool_call> for queries, During tokenization, we map Dseeds query and response tags to Gemmas native tool toand <tool_response> and kens: <tool_response> for responses. Fine-tuning supervises the document text, queries, all four boundary tokens, and the end-of-turn marker, whereas the instruction prefix and retrieved response text are masked from the loss. Supervising the document text teaches the annotator to continue without searching where no call is present. We use the final checkpoint after three epochs to annotate the pretraining corpora and search-SFT data. The same instruction prefix is used during annotation. Annotating pretraining corpus. We run Mϕ over the entire training corpus to identify query insertion points. We keep candidate positions with insertion probability τ 0.05, enforcing minimum separation of 40 characters. Queries are generated using greedy decoding with limit of 24 tokens. The same τ and query-generation budget are used for both Wikipedia and DCLM-Edu. After retrieving and compressing

We retain insertions with score of at least 0.1. Choice of retrieval index. We first evaluate the 100B and 1T-token subsets of FineWeb-Edu as retrieval corpora. Although scaling to 1T tokens improves the query response rate, the 100B-token subset already returns results for 90% of search queries covered by 1T-token subset. We further find that Sphere (Piktus et al., 2022) retrieves more relevant results than the 100B-token FineWeb-Edu subset, as measured by the increase in log-likelihood of the original document continuation immediately following the retrieved results. A.2 TRAINING SETUP Datasets and preprocessing. For Wikipedia, we annotate the 6,083,581 English articles in the November 2023 snapshot (20231101.en). We restrict the corpus to the articles also present in LMLMs Wikipedia set and remove those without accepted search insertion. The final training corpus contains 4.01B original-document tokens and 8.43B tokens after search annotation. We reserve 1% of training corpus as held-out set. For DCLM-Edu, we retain subset of complete files from HuggingFaceTB/dclm-edu, retaining documents with educational scores of 25 without further score-based filtering. We remove documents shorter than 200 characters and exact duplicates within each file. The resulting corpus contains 65.13B original-document tokens and 101.54B tokens after search annotations. We reserve 1% of training corpus as held-out set. Gathering retrieved responses for search annotation, we cap response length to approximately 400 characters for Wikipedia and 800 for DCLM-Edu. We pack documents into 4,096-token blocks using bestfit-decreasing packing, with supervised end-of-text token after each document. Padding and retrieved responses are excluded from the loss; document text and queries are supervised. Model architectures. The Wikipedia models use the SmolLM2-360M configuration, with groupedquery attention, SiLU feed-forward network, and tied input and output embeddings. The DCLM-Edu models use nanochat configurations with full multi-head attention, query/key normalization, squaredReLU feed-forward networks, and untied input and output embeddings. They add gated value embeddings on alternating layers and cap output logits at 15. Wikipedia uses RMSNorm with ϵ = 105; DCLM uses parameter-free RMSNorm. All configurations use rotary position embeddings with base 100,000 and omit biases. Table 3 gives the dimensions and parameter counts. The DCLM model sizes used throughout the paper exclude value embeddings; the table also reports total stored parameters. All models use the SmolLM2 tokenizer extended with four search tokens, giving vocabulary of 49,156 tokens. Nanochat pads the vocabulary dimension to 49,216. For the Wikipedia models, the four new embedding rows are initialized to the mean of the other rows.

Document tokens count the original document tokens, also including repeated passes. The Wikipedia QueryLM trains for four epochs and is compared with an eight-epoch baseline, using approximately 4% more compute. The DCLM-Edu-trained QueryLM at 400M, 1.4B, and 3.3B scales use 6.8B, 28.2B, and 64.0B document tokens, and their compute-matched baselines are trained on more document tokens to run for the same number of steps. Matching compute requires the 3.3B baseline to repeat approximately 34.6B document tokens; the 400M and 1.4B baselines do not repeat documents. The over-trained 400M search model uses the full annotated corpus; its baseline runs 67 additional steps (0.07%) and repeats approximately 36.5B document tokens. Resources. Across QueryLM and baseline model training, pretraining used approximately 316 GPUhours on NVIDIA Hopper GPUs for Wikipedia (16H200) and 2,240 GPU-hours on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs for DCLM-Edu (16B200). These totals exclude annotation, ablations, and the four-epoch Wikipedia reference. GPU-hours sum training time across all devices.

A.3 SEARCH FINE-TUNING Data mixture. QueryLM and Standard are both fine-tuned on approximately 53,000 user-assistant conversations. Of these, about 64% of data split consist of smol-rewrite, smol-summarize, smolconstraints, and everyday-conversations subsets of SmolTalk (Allal et al., 2025), teaching general chat skills and are not augmented with search annotation. Another 15% of data is Hermes function-calling and xLAM subsets of SmolTalk2 (Allal et al., 2025), demonstrating tool calling behavior. The remaining 21% (11,237 conversations) consist of the Magpie, OpenHermes, and SystemChats subsets of SmolTalk and are augmented with search insertions. We remove conversations for which web search is unlikely to be useful, such as fiction, mathematical calculations, code generation, or questions answerable from the prompt. We use the base Llama-3.18B model (Grattafiori et al., 2024), prompted with labeled examples, as binary classifier to make this decision. Search annotation. We annotate conversations with the same annotator, pipeline, and thresholds as for DCLM-Edu pretraining (Section A.1), restricting search augmentation to assistant turns. Search responses are retrieved with BM25 over Sphere and compressed using an 800-character budget. After the initial annotation, we move all inserted search blocks to the start of the sentences in which they were originally placed, retaining at most one block per sentence. This enforces the behavior that an assistant searches before writing claim rather than in the middle of it. Also, this setup matches our evaluation where search is triggered at the start of the assistant turn. The final data contain 38,436 search blocks across 9,713 conversations. The 1,524 conversations left without block are kept as ordinary chat. Format and loss masking. Conversations are rendered as plain text, with System:, User:, and Assistant: role prefixes, with turns separated by blank lines. We add no additional chat tokens. Search blocks use the same query and response tokens as pretraining (Section 3.3). We compute the loss on assistant text, search-query blocks, and end-of-sequence token, while masking and the loss on User turn, system prompts, retrieved responses, and padding. The loss on role prefixes are masked as well, except for the User: to signal end of assistant turn. We pack conversations into 4,096-token sequences using best-fit-decreasing packing, truncating longer conversations. Attention is not masked between conversations in the same sequence. This gives 8,601 sequences with 35.2M tokens, 44% of which carry loss. We reserve 1% split consisting of 87 sequences as held-out set. Optimization. Each corpus is fine-tuned for one epoch with its pretraining trainer  (Table 6)  . For DCLM-Edu models, we follow nanochats fine-tuning recipe. Training resumes from the final pretraining checkpoint together with its optimizer state, including Muon momentum and AdamW moments; only the step counter and data position are reset. A.4 EVALUATION A.4.1 TASKS We evaluate QueryLM and baselines on eight open-ended question-answering tasks that probe world knowledge. Four tasks primarily assess factual recall: TriviaQA covers broad factual knowledge through trivia questions; Natural Questions (NQ-Open) pairs Google search questions with short answers; PopQA tests knowledge derived from Wikipedia knowledge-triplets; and WebQuestions contains question-answer pairs derived from web search queries. The other four tasks assess multi-hop reasoning, requiring models to connect multiple pieces of evidence. HotpotQA requires combining evidence across Wikipedia articles, while 2Wiki emphasizes explicit reasoning chains across Wikipedia facts. MuSiQue constructs questions requiring two to four reasoning steps by composing single-hop questions; we only consider two-hop questions from MuSiQue. Bamboogle contains challenging two-hop questions whose answers are supported by Wikipedia articles. In addition, we use FreshQA to test whether retrieval helps modeles answer questions about current facts. Finally, HaluEval and RAGTruth assess models groundedness in supplied evidence in settings involving hallucinated or unsupported content. A.4.2 EVALUATION BUDGET In the search-enabled setting, model makes one search query per question on the four factual QA tasks and up to two queries per question on the four multi-hop QA tasks. The first query is forced in both settings. Further search queries are suppressed for factual QA, while the second query is optional for multi-hop QA. We use greedy decoding for both base and SFT models, with maximum of 24 tokens per search query. Answer generation is limited to 24 tokens for base models and 64 tokens for SFT models. For each query, we retrieve the top-3 search results using either BM25 over the selected retrieval corpus or Tavily. We extract up to eight relevant sentences from the combined results, using budget of approximately 1,200 characters that preserves complete sentences. A.4.3 PROMPTING For base model evaluation, we use four-shot demonstrations of question and answer pairs sampled from the corresponding task. Closed-book evaluation contain regular question and answer pairs, whereas search-enabled demonstrations includes search and retrieval steps in each models native format: explicit search query and result blocks for QueryLM , fact blocks for Co-LMLM, and entityrelation look-ups for LMLM. For multi-hop tasks, the four-shot demonstrations include both one-search and two-search examples. SFT models are evaluated zero-shot, using User:/Assistant: format to be consistent with their
